claim: Homeodomain transcription factors (HD TFs) are instrumental to vertebrate development.
source: Homeodomain transcription factors (HD TFs) are instrumental to vertebrate development.
evidence: This is a general statement about HD TFs supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Mutations in HD TFs have been linked to human diseases.
source: Mutations in HD TFs have been linked to human diseases, but their pathogenic mechanisms remain elusive.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and established knowledge in the field.

claim: The pathogenic mechanisms of HD TF mutations remain elusive.
source: Mutations in HD TFs have been linked to human diseases, but their pathogenic mechanisms remain elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: p.E80A mutation increases CRX-mediated transactivation of canonical CRX target genes in developing photoreceptors.
source: p.E80A increases CRX-mediated transactivation of canonical CRX target genes in developing photoreceptors
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from luciferase assays and RNA-seq analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: p.K88N mutation alters CRX DNA-binding specificity resulting in binding at ectopic sites.
source: p.K88N alters CRX DNA-binding specificity resulting in binding at ectopic sites and severe perturbation of CRX target gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by Spec-seq and ChIP-seq data showing altered DNA-binding specificity.

claim: p.K88N mutation causes severe perturbation of CRX target gene expression.
source: p.K88N alters CRX DNA-binding specificity resulting in binding at ectopic sites and severe perturbation of CRX target gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing widespread gene expression changes.

claim: Both E80A and K88N mutations produce novel retinal morphological defects.
source: Both mechanisms produce novel retinal morphological defects and hinder photoreceptor maturation distinct from loss-of-function models.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis showing whorls and rosettes in the ONL.

claim: Both E80A and K88N mutations hinder photoreceptor maturation distinct from loss-of-function models.
source: Both mechanisms produce novel retinal morphological defects and hinder photoreceptor maturation distinct from loss-of-function models.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with CrxR90W/W loss-of-function model data.

claim: The homeodomain (HD) is a highly conserved 60 amino acid helix-turn-helix DNA-binding domain.
source: Members of the HD TF family are characterized by the presence of a highly conserved 60 amino acid helix-turn-helix DNA-binding domain known as the homeodomain (HD).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HD structure supported by citations.

claim: The HD was discovered in Drosophila homeotic transformations.
source: The HD is one of the most studied eukaryotic DNA-binding motifs since its discovery in Drosophila homeotic transformations (Mark et al., 1997; Lewis, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical work.

claim: Hundreds of HD TFs have been documented in regulating gene expression programs important for body plan specification, pattern formation, and cell fate determination.
source: Hundreds of HD TFs have subsequently been documented in regulating gene expression programs important for body plan specification, pattern formation, and cell fate determination (Mark et al., 1997; Lewis, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Mutations in HD TFs have been linked to neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative conditions.
source: Mutations in HD TFs have been linked to many human diseases, including neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative conditions (Leung et al., 2022; Chi, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The retina has long been used as a model system to study the role of HD TFs in normal central nervous system development and in neurological diseases.
source: The retina has long been used as a model system to study the role of HD TFs in normal central nervous system development and in neurological diseases (Zagozewski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: HD TFs play essential roles in the patterning of neuroepithelium, specification of retinal progenitors and differentiation of all retinal cell classes during retinogenesis.
source: During retinogenesis, HD TFs play essential roles in the patterning of neuroepithelium, specification of retinal progenitors and differentiation of all retinal cell classes that derive from a common progenitor (Diacou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Many HD TFs are shared between the brain and the retina during development.
source: Importantly, many HD TFs are shared between the brain and the retina during development and mutations in these TFs can lead to disease manifestation in both tissues (Beby and Lamonerie, 2013; Henderson et al., 2009; Abouzeid et al., 2009; Lima Cunha et al., 2019; Voronina et al., 2004; Abouzeid et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Mutations in HD TFs shared between brain and retina can lead to disease manifestation in both tissues.
source: Importantly, many HD TFs are shared between the brain and the retina during development and mutations in these TFs can lead to disease manifestation in both tissues (Beby and Lamonerie, 2013; Henderson et al., 2009; Abouzeid et al., 2009; Lima Cunha et al., 2019; Voronina et al., 2004; Abouzeid et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: CRX is a HD TF essential for photoreceptor cells in the retina.
source: Here, we study CRX, a HD TF essential for photoreceptor cells in the retina, as a model to understand how single amino acid substitutions in the HD impact TF functions and cause blinding diseases.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: Photoreceptors are the most numerous neurons in the retina.
source: Photoreceptors are the most numerous neurons in the retina and are specialized to sense light and initiate vision through a process called phototransduction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about retinal anatomy.

claim: Photoreceptors are specialized to sense light and initiate vision through phototransduction.
source: Photoreceptors are the most numerous neurons in the retina and are specialized to sense light and initiate vision through a process called phototransduction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about photoreceptor function.

claim: Crx is first expressed in post-mitotic photoreceptor precursors.
source: Animal studies have demonstrated that Crx is first expressed in post-mitotic photoreceptor precursors (Muranishi et al., 2011) and maintained throughout life (Chen et al., 1997; Furukawa et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Crx expression is maintained throughout life.
source: Animal studies have demonstrated that Crx is first expressed in post-mitotic photoreceptor precursors (Muranishi et al., 2011) and maintained throughout life (Chen et al., 1997; Furukawa et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Loss of CRX results in impaired photoreceptor gene expression.
source: Loss of CRX results in impaired photoreceptor gene expression, failure of maturation and rapid degeneration of immature, non-functional photoreceptors (Furukawa et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on CRX knockout.

claim: Loss of CRX results in failure of photoreceptor maturation.
source: Loss of CRX results in impaired photoreceptor gene expression, failure of maturation and rapid degeneration of immature, non-functional photoreceptors (Furukawa et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on CRX knockout.

claim: Loss of CRX results in rapid degeneration of immature, non-functional photoreceptors.
source: Loss of CRX results in impaired photoreceptor gene expression, failure of maturation and rapid degeneration of immature, non-functional photoreceptors (Furukawa et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on CRX knockout.

claim: Protein-coding sequence variants in human CRX have been associated with Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA).
source: Protein-coding sequence variants in human CRX have been associated with inherited retinal diseases (IRDs) that affect photoreceptors: Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA), cone–rod dystrophy (CoRD), and retinitis pigmentosa (RP) (OMIM:602225).
evidence: This is supported by reference to OMIM database.

claim: Protein-coding sequence variants in human CRX have been associated with cone–rod dystrophy (CoRD).
source: Protein-coding sequence variants in human CRX have been associated with inherited retinal diseases (IRDs) that affect photoreceptors: Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA), cone–rod dystrophy (CoRD), and retinitis pigmentosa (RP) (OMIM:602225).
evidence: This is supported by reference to OMIM database.

claim: Protein-coding sequence variants in human CRX have been associated with retinitis pigmentosa (RP).
source: Protein-coding sequence variants in human CRX have been associated with inherited retinal diseases (IRDs) that affect photoreceptors: Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA), cone–rod dystrophy (CoRD), and retinitis pigmentosa (RP) (OMIM:602225).
evidence: This is supported by reference to OMIM database.

claim: The recessive phenotype observed in Crx knockout mouse models fails to recapitulate many dominant human CRX mutations that arise de novo.
source: However, the recessive phenotype observed in Crx knockout mouse models fails to recapitulate many dominant human CRX mutations that arise de novo (Furukawa et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation and comparison of mouse and human phenotypes.

claim: CRX contains an N-terminal HD and C-terminal activation domain (AD).
source: CRX contains two functional domains – the N-terminal HD and C-terminal activation domain (AD) (Figure 1A), both are required for proper activation of target genes and maintenance of normal Crx mRNA transcript abundance (Chau et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Both CRX HD and AD are required for proper activation of target genes.
source: CRX contains two functional domains – the N-terminal HD and C-terminal activation domain (AD) (Figure 1A), both are required for proper activation of target genes and maintenance of normal Crx mRNA transcript abundance (Chau et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Both CRX HD and AD are required for maintenance of normal Crx mRNA transcript abundance.
source: CRX contains two functional domains – the N-terminal HD and C-terminal activation domain (AD) (Figure 1A), both are required for proper activation of target genes and maintenance of normal Crx mRNA transcript abundance (Chau et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: R90W mutation produces a recessive loss-of-function phenotype very similar to that of Crx knockout mice.
source: We found that R90W mutation produces a recessive loss-of-function phenotype very similar to that of Crx knockout mice.
evidence: This is supported by data from the previous study on R90W knock-in mice.

claim: E80A, K88N, and R90W mutations are located at the C-terminus of CRX HD.
source: The three missense mutations in this study are located at the C-terminus of CRX HD and associated with different retinal diseases in human.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: E80A, K88N, and R90W mutations are associated with different retinal diseases in human.
source: The three missense mutations in this study are located at the C-terminus of CRX HD and associated with different retinal diseases in human.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and supported by citations.

claim: Missense variants E80A, K88N, and R90W are located at highly conserved residues across species and different HD transcription factors.
source: Missense variants in this study (highlighted) are located at highly conserved residues across species and different HD transcription factors (TFs).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B through sequence alignment.

claim: CRX belongs to the paired-like HD TF family that recognize a 6-bp DNA motif.
source: CRX belongs to the paired-like HD TF family that recognize a 6-bp DNA motif in a stereotypic way (Desplan et al., 1988; Trelsman et al., 1989; Hanes and Brent, 1989; Hanes and Brent, 1991; Ades and Sauer, 1995; Wilson et al., 1995; Gehring et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: Recognition of the 3′ region (bases 4–6) of the HD DNA-binding site is mediated by specificity determinants within the conserved HD recognition helix.
source: Extensive studies of the HD have revealed a canonical HD–DNA recognition model where recognition of the 3′ region (bases 4–6) of the HD DNA-binding site is mediated by specificity determinants within the conserved HD recognition helix, corresponding to CRX residues 80–96 (Desplan et al., 1988; Trelsman et al., 1989; Hanes and Brent, 1989; Hanes and Brent, 1991; Gehring et al., 1994; Noyes et al., 2008; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural studies and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: HD residue 50, equivalent to CRX K88 residue, is the major specificity determinant in paired-like HD TF–DNA interactions.
source: In particular, HD residue 50, equivalent to CRX K88 residue (Figure 1A), is the major specificity determinant in paired-like HD TF–DNA interactions (Trelsman et al., 1989; Hanes and Brent, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Relative binding energies of CRX WT HD from two Spec-seq experiments showed strong correlation (r: 0.984).
source: Relative binding energies of CRX WT HD from two experiments showed strong correlation (r: 0.984) and noise level (0.114 kT) within the expected range in typical Spec-seq data (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F with quantitative data.

claim: The noise level in WT CRX HD Spec-seq experiments (0.114 kT) is within the expected range in typical Spec-seq data.
source: Relative binding energies of CRX WT HD from two experiments showed strong correlation (r: 0.984) and noise level (0.114 kT) within the expected range in typical Spec-seq data (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: WT CRX HD shows a clear preference for CC bases at the 3′ end of the motif.
source: A clear preference for CC bases at the 3′ end of the motif is consistent with known CRX-binding preference in vitro and in vivo (Corbo et al., 2010; Kwasnieski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G and supported by citations.

claim: R90W HD bound with slightly higher specificity than WT.
source: R90W HD bound with slightly higher specificity than WT, as demonstrated by most data points falling above the identity line (Figure 1H, K), suggesting that R90W HD is more sensitive than WT to binding sequence variations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H and 1K with quantitative comparison.

claim: R90W HD is more sensitive than WT to binding sequence variations.
source: R90W HD bound with slightly higher specificity than WT, as demonstrated by most data points falling above the identity line (Figure 1H, K), suggesting that R90W HD is more sensitive than WT to binding sequence variations.
evidence: This is inferred from the Spec-seq data shown in Figure 1H and 1K.

claim: E80A HD bound with lower specificity than WT HD.
source: In contrast, when comparing E80A HD with WT HD, many data points fell below the identity line and the relative binding energies regressed toward 0 on the E80A axis (Figure 1I, L). This suggests that E80A HD bound with lower specificity than WT HD and thus was more tolerant to base variations in the HD DNA motif.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1I and 1L with quantitative comparison.

claim: E80A HD was more tolerant to base variations in the HD DNA motif than WT.
source: In contrast, when comparing E80A HD with WT HD, many data points fell below the identity line and the relative binding energies regressed toward 0 on the E80A axis (Figure 1I, L). This suggests that E80A HD bound with lower specificity than WT HD and thus was more tolerant to base variations in the HD DNA motif.
evidence: This is inferred from the Spec-seq data shown in Figure 1I and 1L.

claim: K88N mutation dramatically altered CRX HD DNA-binding specificity (r: 0.160).
source: Different from R90W and E80A, K88N mutation dramatically altered CRX HD DNA-binding specificity (r: 0.160) (Figure 1J, M).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1J and 1M with quantitative comparison showing low correlation.

claim: K88N HD preferred binding sequence is TAAT/ATT/A.
source: The K88N preferred binding sequence (TAAT/ATT/A) is referred to as N88 HD motif hereafter.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1M.

claim: K88N HD had the largest degree of discrimination from its preferred to the weakest binding motif.
source: K88N HD also had the largest degree of discrimination from its preferred to the weakest binding motif, suggesting that it is most sensitive to variants in the HD DNA motif.
evidence: This is inferred from the Spec-seq data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: K88N HD is most sensitive to variants in the HD DNA motif.
source: K88N HD also had the largest degree of discrimination from its preferred to the weakest binding motif, suggesting that it is most sensitive to variants in the HD DNA motif.
evidence: This is inferred from the Spec-seq data.

claim: E80A mutation does not affect CRX HD DNA-binding specificity.
source: Together, these results indicate that while E80A mutation does not affect CRX HD DNA-binding specificity, the K88N mutation dramatically alters the specificity in vitro.
evidence: This is concluded from the Spec-seq experiments showing E80A prefers the same consensus as WT.

claim: K88N mutation dramatically alters CRX HD DNA-binding specificity in vitro.
source: Together, these results indicate that while E80A mutation does not affect CRX HD DNA-binding specificity, the K88N mutation dramatically alters the specificity in vitro.
evidence: This is concluded from the Spec-seq experiments showing K88N prefers a different consensus.

claim: Crx mRNA was expressed at comparable levels in WT and mutant retinas.
source: We confirmed that Crx mRNA was expressed at comparable levels in WT and mutant retinas (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C with qRT-PCR data.

claim: Full-length CRX proteins were readily detectable in the nuclear extracts from all samples.
source: and the full-length CRX proteins were readily detectable in the nuclear extracts from all samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D with Western blot data.

claim: ChIP-seq was performed on mouse retinas at P14.
source: We then obtained genome-wide binding profiles for each CRX variant by chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) on mouse retinas at P14, a time when all retinal cell types are born, photoreceptor specification is completed in WT animals, and prior to any observed cell death in other CRX mutants previously characterized (Tran et al., 2014; Bassett and Wallace, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the methods description.

claim: At P14, all retinal cell types are born in WT animals.
source: We then obtained genome-wide binding profiles for each CRX variant by chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) on mouse retinas at P14, a time when all retinal cell types are born, photoreceptor specification is completed in WT animals, and prior to any observed cell death in other CRX mutants previously characterized (Tran et al., 2014; Bassett and Wallace, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to developmental studies.

claim: At P14, photoreceptor specification is completed in WT animals.
source: We then obtained genome-wide binding profiles for each CRX variant by chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) on mouse retinas at P14, a time when all retinal cell types are born, photoreceptor specification is completed in WT animals, and prior to any observed cell death in other CRX mutants previously characterized (Tran et al., 2014; Bassett and Wallace, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to developmental studies.

claim: P14 is prior to any observed cell death in other CRX mutants previously characterized.
source: We then obtained genome-wide binding profiles for each CRX variant by chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) on mouse retinas at P14, a time when all retinal cell types are born, photoreceptor specification is completed in WT animals, and prior to any observed cell death in other CRX mutants previously characterized (Tran et al., 2014; Bassett and Wallace, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous CRX mutant studies.

claim: CRX E80A protein binds to canonical WT CRX-binding sites.
source: Cluster 1 consisted of canonical WT CRX-binding sites that are also occupied by CRX E80A protein (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and 2B with ChIP-seq data.

claim: CRX E80A-binding in vivo was mostly enriched in intronic regions, followed by intergenic and transcription start site (TSS) regions.
source: Similar to WT CRX, CRX E80A-binding in vivo was mostly enriched in intronic, followed by intergenic and transcription start site (TSS) regions (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D (likely meant Figure 2D based on context) with genomic distribution analysis.

claim: CRX R90W failed to produce significant DNA binding in vivo.
source: In contrast, CRX R90W, that also showed similar consensus preference to WT in vitro, failed to produce significant DNA binding in vivo (Figure 2A–C, Methods).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A-C with ChIP-seq data.

claim: The retinopathy phenotype of CrxR90W/W is likely due to loss of binding at canonical WT CRX-binding sites.
source: This suggests that the retinopathy phenotype of CrxR90W/W is likely due to loss of binding at canonical WT CRX-binding sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing loss of binding.

claim: CRX K88N showed loss of binding at canonical CRX-binding sites.
source: Intriguingly, while CRX K88N showed loss of binding at canonical CRX-binding sites, it gained a small set of binding sites (Cluster 2, Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A-C with ChIP-seq data.

claim: CRX K88N gained a small set of binding sites (Cluster 2).
source: Intriguingly, while CRX K88N showed loss of binding at canonical CRX-binding sites, it gained a small set of binding sites (Cluster 2, Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A-C with ChIP-seq data.

claim: De novo motif searching revealed enrichment of monomeric HD motifs under CRX peaks in each genotype.
source: De novo motif searching with DREME (Bailey, 2011) under CRX peaks in each genotype revealed enrichment of monomeric HD motifs (Figure 2E) consistent with those found in Spec-seq (Figure 1G, K–M)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E with motif analysis.

claim: The enriched HD motifs in ChIP-seq are consistent with those found in Spec-seq.
source: De novo motif searching with DREME (Bailey, 2011) under CRX peaks in each genotype revealed enrichment of monomeric HD motifs (Figure 2E) consistent with those found in Spec-seq (Figure 1G, K–M)
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figure 2E with Figure 1G, K-M.

claim: There is a change in enriched HD motif from WT CRX HD type to N88 HD type in the CrxK88N/N retinas.
source: highlighted by a change in enriched HD motif from WT CRX HD type to N88 HD type in the CrxK88N/N retinas.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E with motif analysis.

claim: In vivo changes in CRX chromatin binding were at least in part driven by the intrinsic changes in HD DNA-binding specificity by each individual mutation.
source: Consistency with in vitro binding models suggests that in vivo changes in CRX chromatin binding were at least in part driven by the intrinsic changes in HD DNA-binding specificity by each individual mutation.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency between Spec-seq and ChIP-seq results.

claim: P10 WT sample showed strong correlations with all developmental ages in the published WT control dataset.
source: As expected, our P10 WT sample showed strong correlations with all developmental ages in the published WT control dataset.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with correlation analysis.

claim: P10 WT sample showed stronger correlation with early ages (P3, P7, P10) and weaker correlation with later ages (P14, P21).
source: A stronger correlation with early ages (P3, P7, P10) and a weaker correlation with later ages (P14, P21) is also an indication of ongoing photoreceptor differentiation at P10.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and interpreted as ongoing differentiation.

claim: CrxE80A/+ and CrxE80A/A samples showed stronger correlation with later developmental ages (P14, P21) but weaker correlation with earlier postnatal ages (P3, P7).
source: Unlike the WT sample, CrxE80A/+ and CrxE80A/A samples both showed a stronger correlation with later developmental ages (P14, P21) but a weaker correlation with earlier postnatal ages (P3, P7).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with correlation analysis.

claim: CRX-DAGs were prematurely upregulated in the P10 CrxE80A/+ and CrxE80A/A mutant retinas.
source: Since the CRX-DAGs are normally developmentally upregulated, this shift in correlation toward later developmental ages suggested that these genes were prematurely upregulated in the P10 CrxE80A/+ and CrxE80A/A mutant retinas.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CrxK88N/+ and CrxK88N/N samples showed weaker correlation with all developmental ages when compared with WT samples.
source: In contrast, CrxK88N/+ and CrxK88N/N samples both showed a weaker correlation with all developmental ages when compared with WT samples in our dataset.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with correlation analysis.

claim: Early photoreceptor differentiation was compromised in both CrxK88N mutants.
source: This suggests that early photoreceptor differentiation was compromised in both CrxK88N mutants, consistent with their association with early-onset LCA (Nichols et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation analysis and supported by citation to clinical phenotype.

claim: CrxR90W/W displayed strong correlation with earlier ages (P3, P7) similar to WT, but only showed moderate correlation with later ages (P14, P21).
source: Importantly, CrxR90W/W, also associated with LCA-like phenotype (Tran et al., 2014; Swaroop et al., 1999), displayed strong correlation with earlier ages (P3, P7) similar to WT, but only showed moderate correlation with later ages (P14, P21).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with correlation analysis.

claim: Loss of CRX function at canonical binding sites does not affect the initiation of photoreceptor differentiation.
source: This suggests loss of CRX function at canonical binding sites does not affect the initiation of photoreceptor differentiation, but WT CRX activity at these sites is required to sustain differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation pattern of CrxR90W/W.

claim: WT CRX activity at canonical binding sites is required to sustain photoreceptor differentiation.
source: This suggests loss of CRX function at canonical binding sites does not affect the initiation of photoreceptor differentiation, but WT CRX activity at these sites is required to sustain differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation pattern of CrxR90W/W.

claim: CRX-DAG expression was more severely affected in CrxK88N mutants than in CrxR90W/W.
source: Since CRX-DAG expression was more severely affected in CrxK88N mutants than in CrxR90W/W, the photoreceptor differentiation deficits seen in the CrxK88N mutants cannot be explained solely by the loss of regulatory activity at canonical CRX-binding sites.
evidence: This is shown by comparing gene expression data between mutants.

claim: The photoreceptor differentiation deficits seen in the CrxK88N mutants cannot be explained solely by the loss of regulatory activity at canonical CRX-binding sites.
source: Since CRX-DAG expression was more severely affected in CrxK88N mutants than in CrxR90W/W, the photoreceptor differentiation deficits seen in the CrxK88N mutants cannot be explained solely by the loss of regulatory activity at canonical CRX-binding sites.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the severity of phenotypes.

claim: E80A and K88N mutations affected the expression of CRX-dependent activated genes in opposite directions.
source: Overall, our sample-wise correlation analysis with normal retinal development dataset suggests that E80A and K88N mutations affected the expression CRX-dependent activated genes in opposite directions, implicating novel and distinct pathogenic mechanisms from the loss-of-function R90W mutation.
evidence: This is concluded from the correlation analysis and gene expression data.

claim: E80A and K88N mutations implicate novel and distinct pathogenic mechanisms from the loss-of-function R90W mutation.
source: Overall, our sample-wise correlation analysis with normal retinal development dataset suggests that E80A and K88N mutations affected the expression CRX-dependent activated genes in opposite directions, implicating novel and distinct pathogenic mechanisms from the loss-of-function R90W mutation.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive analysis of all three mutants.

claim: Group 1 genes were upregulated in CrxE80A mutants compared to WT.
source: In aggregate, when compared to WT, Group 1 genes were upregulated in CrxE80A mutants while Group 2 genes were downregulated.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B with hierarchical clustering of gene expression.

claim: Group 2 genes were downregulated in CrxE80A mutants compared to WT.
source: In aggregate, when compared to WT, Group 1 genes were upregulated in CrxE80A mutants while Group 2 genes were downregulated.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B with hierarchical clustering of gene expression.

claim: Genes indicative of rods and cones could partially define Group 1 and Group 2.
source: We noted genes indicative of the two photoreceptor subtypes, rods and cones, could partially define the two groups (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and 3D with gene expression patterns.

claim: Esrrb is an important regulator of rod differentiation.
source: For example, Esrrb (Onishi et al., 2010) and Nrl (Yoshida et al., 2004) in Group 1 are important regulators of rod differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Nrl is an important regulator of rod differentiation.
source: For example, Esrrb (Onishi et al., 2010) and Nrl (Yoshida et al., 2004) in Group 1 are important regulators of rod differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Peaks associated with Group 2 genes showed lower occupancy compared to Group 1 genes in the CrxE80A/A retinas.
source: Comparison of ChIP-seq signal revealed that peaks associated with Group 2 genes showed lower occupancy compared to Group 1 genes in the CrxE80A/A retinas (Mann–Whitney U-test p-value: 9.51e−07)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A with statistical analysis.

claim: No difference in ChIP-seq signal was observed between Group 1 and Group 2 genes in WT retinas.
source: while no difference was observed in WT retinas (Mann–Whitney U-test p-value: 0.541)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A with statistical analysis.

claim: Loss of CRX activity likely underlies the downregulation of Group 2 genes in the CrxE80A mutants.
source: suggesting loss of CRX activity likely underlies the downregulation of Group 2 genes in the CrxE80A mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq occupancy data.

claim: The selective downregulation of cone genes in Group 2 may explain the CoRD-like phenotype in adult CrxE80A mutant mice.
source: Collectively, the selective downregulation of cone genes in Group 2 may explain the CoRD-like phenotype in adult CrxE80A mutant mice described later.
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression patterns and phenotype correlation.

claim: A subset of CRX-independent genes were downregulated in CrxE80A mutants.
source: Additionally, we noticed that a subset of genes not affected in CrxR90W/W (CRX-independent genes) were also downregulated in CrxE80A mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-D with gene expression data.

claim: Ascl1 is a transcription regulator important for early photoreceptor development.
source: Among these genes were transcription regulators important for early photoreceptor development, such as Ascl1 (Kaufman et al., 2019), Rax (Irie et al., 2015), Sall3 (de Melo et al., 2011), and Pias3 (Onishi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a functional study.

claim: The downregulation of early photoreceptor development factors coincided with the upregulation of mature rod genes in P10 CrxE80A retinas.
source: The downregulation of these factors coincided with the upregulation of mature rod genes in P10 CrxE80A retinas, suggesting that the E80A mutation might hamper the proper timing of photoreceptor differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression patterns.

claim: The E80A mutation might hamper the proper timing of photoreceptor differentiation.
source: The downregulation of these factors coincided with the upregulation of mature rod genes in P10 CrxE80A retinas, suggesting that the E80A mutation might hamper the proper timing of photoreceptor differentiation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the gene expression patterns.

claim: CrxK88N retinas had the most severe gene expression changes among all mutants.
source: CrxK88N retinas had the most severe gene expression changes among all mutants with downregulation of both Group 1 (rod) and Group 2 (cone) genes (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B-D with gene expression data.

claim: The heterozygous CrxK88N/+ retina displayed a similar degree of expression reduction as homozygous CrxR90W/W.
source: The heterozygous CrxK88N/+ retina displayed a similar degree of expression reduction as homozygous CrxR90W/W, consistent with its association with dLCA (Nichols et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown by comparing gene expression data and supported by citation to clinical phenotype.

claim: Mutant CRX K88N not only failed to activate WT target genes, but also functionally antagonized WT CRX regulatory activity in differentiating photoreceptors.
source: Given the normal phenotype of heterozygous loss-of-function mutants – Crx+/− and CrxR90W/+, these results suggest that mutant CRX K88N not only failed to activate WT target genes, but also functionally antagonized WT CRX regulatory activity in differentiating photoreceptors (Tran et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing heterozygous phenotypes and supported by citation.

claim: CrxK88N/N retina displayed a more severe expression reduction of CRX-DAG than CrxR90W/W.
source: In the absence of WT CRX, CrxK88N/N retina displayed a more severe expression reduction of CRX-DAG than CrxR90W/W
evidence: This is shown by comparing gene expression data.

claim: CRX K88N antagonized the activity of other transcriptional regulators important for photoreceptor differentiation.
source: raising the possibility that CRX K88N also antagonized the activity of other transcriptional regulators important for photoreceptor differentiation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the severity of the phenotype.

claim: A set of CRX-independent genes were mis-regulated in both heterozygous and homozygous CrxK88N mutants.
source: Supporting this possibility, a set of CRX-independent genes were also mis-regulated in both heterozygous and homozygous CrxK88N mutants.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E with gene expression data.

claim: CRX K88N is associated with greater gene expression changes than other CRX HD mutants.
source: Overall, CRX K88N is associated with greater gene expression changes than other CRX HD mutants, which is likely attributed to ectopic regulatory activity.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive gene expression analysis.

claim: The greater gene expression changes in CRX K88N mutants are likely attributed to ectopic regulatory activity.
source: Overall, CRX K88N is associated with greater gene expression changes than other CRX HD mutants, which is likely attributed to ectopic regulatory activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing ectopic binding.

claim: At P21, the normal retina has largely completed terminal differentiation with photoreceptor gene expression reaching a plateau.
source: At this age, the normal retina has largely completed terminal differentiation with photoreceptor gene expression reaching a plateau (Aavani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a developmental study.

claim: Many genes in the GO term detection of light stimulus failed to reach WT levels in P21 CRX HD mutant retinas.
source: However, when P21 CRX HD mutant retinas were examined for the expression of genes under the GO term detection of light stimulus (GO:0009583), which comprises genes in both rod and cone phototransduction cascades, many genes failed to reach WT levels, despite variable degrees of impact across different HD mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A with gene expression data.

claim: CrxE80A mutants displayed a deficiency in both cone and rod phototransduction genes at P21.
source: CrxE80A mutants, in contrast to the increased rod gene expression at P10, displayed a deficiency in both cone and rod phototransduction genes at P21 (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B with gene expression data.

claim: Mutant CRX E80A transcriptional activity fails to sustain photoreceptor terminal differentiation.
source: This suggests that mutant CRX E80A transcriptional activity fails to sustain photoreceptor terminal differentiation and ultimately results in non-functional and severely affected photoreceptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression patterns at P21.

claim: CrxK88N mutants showed severely reduced expression of rod/cone phototransduction genes at both P10 and P21.
source: In comparison, CrxK88N mutants showed severely reduced expression of rod/cone phototransduction genes at both P10 and P21 (Figures 3B–D–4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3B-D and 4B with gene expression data.

claim: All mutants showed variable degrees of ONL disorganization, forming waves, whorls, and rosettes.
source: Compared to the well-organized ONL in WT retinas (Figure 5A), all mutants showed variable degrees of ONL disorganization, forming waves, whorls, and rosettes (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A-E with histological images.

claim: The ONL disorganization was more severe in homozygotes than in heterozygotes for both E80A and K88N mutations.
source: The ONL disorganization was more severe in homozygotes than in heterozygotes for both mutations and CrxK88N mutants were more severely affected than CrxE80A mutants.
evidence: This is observed from the histological images in Figure 5.

claim: CrxK88N mutants were more severely affected than CrxE80A mutants in terms of ONL disorganization.
source: The ONL disorganization was more severe in homozygotes than in heterozygotes for both mutations and CrxK88N mutants were more severely affected than CrxE80A mutants.
evidence: This is observed from the histological images in Figure 5.

claim: Photoreceptor OS layer was formed in the CrxE80A/+ retinas.
source: Photoreceptor OS layer was formed in the CrxE80A/+ retinas, but absent in CrxE80A/A, CrxK88N/+, and CrxK88N/N mutant retinas.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 with histological images.

claim: Photoreceptor OS layer was absent in CrxE80A/A, CrxK88N/+, and CrxK88N/N mutant retinas.
source: Photoreceptor OS layer was formed in the CrxE80A/+ retinas, but absent in CrxE80A/A, CrxK88N/+, and CrxK88N/N mutant retinas.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 with histological images.

claim: Inner retinal layers were not as severely affected as the outer retinal layers in the mutants.
source: Inner retinal layers, including inner plexiform layer (IPL) and ganglion cell layer were not as severely affected as the outer retinal layers, supporting a model that the mutant morphological abnormalities largely originated from the diseased photoreceptors.
evidence: This is observed from the histological images in Figure 5.

claim: The mutant morphological abnormalities largely originated from the diseased photoreceptors.
source: Inner retinal layers, including inner plexiform layer (IPL) and ganglion cell layer were not as severely affected as the outer retinal layers, supporting a model that the mutant morphological abnormalities largely originated from the diseased photoreceptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential severity of defects in different retinal layers.

claim: The morphological abnormalities in E80A and K88N mutants were distinct from the degenerative phenotypes of other Crx mutant models reported previously.
source: These morphological abnormalities were distinct from the degenerative phenotypes of other Crx mutant models reported previously (Tran et al., 2014; Tran and Chen, 2014; Roger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All mutants lacked mCAR immunoreactivity.
source: Unlike WT retina, all mutants lacked mCAR immunoreactivity (Figure 5G–J), consistent with the loss of cone gene expression shown by RNAseq (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G-J with immunostaining.

claim: The lack of mCAR immunoreactivity in mutants is consistent with the loss of cone gene expression shown by RNAseq.
source: Unlike WT retina, all mutants lacked mCAR immunoreactivity (Figure 5G–J), consistent with the loss of cone gene expression shown by RNAseq (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by comparing immunostaining with RNA-seq data.

claim: In CrxE80A/+ retinas, RHO staining was localized to the OS layer.
source: In CrxE80A/+ retinas, RHO staining was localized to the OS layer; in CrxE80A/A and CrxK88N/+ retinas, positive RHO staining was observed within the whorls and rosettes; in CrxK88N/N mutant retinas, RHO staining was completely absent.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 with immunostaining.

claim: In CrxE80A/A and CrxK88N/+ retinas, positive RHO staining was observed within the whorls and rosettes.
source: In CrxE80A/+ retinas, RHO staining was localized to the OS layer; in CrxE80A/A and CrxK88N/+ retinas, positive RHO staining was observed within the whorls and rosettes; in CrxK88N/N mutant retinas, RHO staining was completely absent.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 with immunostaining.

claim: In CrxK88N/N mutant retinas, RHO staining was completely absent.
source: In CrxE80A/+ retinas, RHO staining was localized to the OS layer; in CrxE80A/A and CrxK88N/+ retinas, positive RHO staining was observed within the whorls and rosettes; in CrxK88N/N mutant retinas, RHO staining was completely absent.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 with immunostaining.

claim: Mis-localized RHO staining was not observed in the inner retinal layers (INL).
source: Importantly, we did not observe mis-localized RHO staining in the inner retinal layers (INL) suggesting that the developmental programs of other retinal cell types were not directly affected by E80A or K88N mutation.
evidence: This is observed from the immunostaining images.

claim: The developmental programs of other retinal cell types were not directly affected by E80A or K88N mutation.
source: Importantly, we did not observe mis-localized RHO staining in the inner retinal layers (INL) suggesting that the developmental programs of other retinal cell types were not directly affected by E80A or K88N mutation.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of mis-localized RHO staining.

claim: Abnormalities in the cone/rod gene expression matched the corresponding human disease diagnosis.
source: Overall, abnormalities in the cone/rod gene expression matched the corresponding human disease diagnosis (Freund et al., 1997; Nichols et al., 2010), and the phenotypic severity correlated with the degree of mis-regulation of CRX target genes in the corresponding RNAseq dataset.
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies and correlation with RNA-seq data.

claim: The phenotypic severity correlated with the degree of mis-regulation of CRX target genes in the corresponding RNAseq dataset.
source: Overall, abnormalities in the cone/rod gene expression matched the corresponding human disease diagnosis (Freund et al., 1997; Nichols et al., 2010), and the phenotypic severity correlated with the degree of mis-regulation of CRX target genes in the corresponding RNAseq dataset.
evidence: This is shown by comparing phenotype severity with gene expression changes.

claim: CRX HD mutation-mediated mis-regulation of gene expression disrupts photoreceptor terminal differentiation.
source: Thus, these results support a model that CRX HD mutation-mediated mis-regulation of gene expression disrupts photoreceptor terminal differentiation and leads to defects in retinal layer organization and OS formation.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive analysis of gene expression and phenotypes.

claim: CRX HD mutation-mediated mis-regulation of gene expression leads to defects in retinal layer organization and OS formation.
source: Thus, these results support a model that CRX HD mutation-mediated mis-regulation of gene expression disrupts photoreceptor terminal differentiation and leads to defects in retinal layer organization and OS formation.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive analysis of gene expression and phenotypes.

claim: CrxE80A/A, CrxK88N/+, and CrxK88N/N mice had no detectable dark- or light-adapted ERG responses.
source: The three severe mutants, CrxE80A/A, CrxK88N/+, and CrxK88N/N had no detectable dark- or light-adapted ERG responses, suggesting that these mice have no rod or cone function and are blind at young ages.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5K-M with ERG data.

claim: CrxE80A/A, CrxK88N/+, and CrxK88N/N mice have no rod or cone function and are blind at young ages.
source: The three severe mutants, CrxE80A/A, CrxK88N/+, and CrxK88N/N had no detectable dark- or light-adapted ERG responses, suggesting that these mice have no rod or cone function and are blind at young ages.
evidence: This is inferred from the ERG data showing no responses.

claim: The null ERG phenotype of the CrxK88N animals is consistent with the clinical LCA phenotype in humans.
source: The null ERG phenotype of the CrxK88N animals is consistent with the clinical LCA phenotype in humans (Nichols et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical study.

claim: CrxE80A/+ animals retained partial rod ERG responses as indicated by the reduced A- and B-wave amplitudes.
source: In contrast, CrxE80A/+ animals retained partial rod ERG responses as indicated by the reduced A- and B-wave amplitudes (Figure 5K, L).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5K and 5L with ERG data.

claim: CrxE80A/+ animals had no detectable cone ERG responses.
source: Yet, CrxE80A/+ animals had no detectable cone ERG responses, which is consistent with the CoRD clinical phenotype in humans (Freund et al., 1997; Figure 5M).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5M with ERG data.

claim: The lack of cone ERG responses in CrxE80A/+ animals is consistent with the CoRD clinical phenotype in humans.
source: Yet, CrxE80A/+ animals had no detectable cone ERG responses, which is consistent with the CoRD clinical phenotype in humans (Freund et al., 1997; Figure 5M).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical study.

claim: The visual function impairment in each CRX HD mutant model coincided with the morphological and molecular changes.
source: Taken together, the visual function impairment in each CRX HD mutant model, coincided with the morphological and molecular changes, suggesting that CrxE80A and CrxK88N mouse models recapitulate the corresponding human diseases.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive analysis of ERG, histology, and gene expression.

claim: CrxE80A and CrxK88N mouse models recapitulate the corresponding human diseases.
source: Taken together, the visual function impairment in each CRX HD mutant model, coincided with the morphological and molecular changes, suggesting that CrxE80A and CrxK88N mouse models recapitulate the corresponding human diseases.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive analysis showing consistency with human phenotypes.

claim: Reporter assays with the Rhodopsin promoter in HEK293T cells can measure changes of CRX transactivation activity.
source: Previous studies have established that reporter assays with the Rhodopsin promoter in HEK293T cells can measure changes of CRX transactivation activity and inform the mechanisms by which photoreceptor genes are mis-regulated in CRX mutant retinas (Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: R90W mutant had significantly reduced activity compared to WT CRX in luciferase assays.
source: Consistent with published studies, R90W mutant had significantly reduced activity compared to WT CRX (Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A with luciferase assay data and supported by citation.

claim: K88N mutant showed a similarly reduced activity as R90W in luciferase assays.
source: K88N mutant showed a similarly reduced activity as R90W, consistent with K88N's loss of binding at canonical CRX sites and failure to activate CRX-DAGs in vivo (Figures 2A, B, 3A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A with luciferase assay data.

claim: E80A mutant showed significantly increased transactivation activity on the Rho promoter.
source: In contrast, E80A mutant, which binds to canonical CRX sties, showed significantly increased transactivation activity on the Rho promoter.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A with luciferase assay data.

claim: The hyperactivity of E80A protein at Rho promoter correlates with the upregulation of CRX-DAGs in the mutant retinas at P10.
source: This hyperactivity of E80A protein at Rho promoter correlates with the upregulation of CRX-DAGs in the mutant retinas at P10 (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is shown by comparing luciferase assay data with RNA-seq data.

claim: RHO proteins were detected by IHC starting around P7 in WT retinas.
source: Previous studies showed that RHO proteins were detected by IHC starting around P7 in WT retinas (Aavani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a developmental study.

claim: Both CrxE80A/+ and CrxE80A/A retinas showed positive RHO staining at P3.
source: In comparison, both CrxE80A/+ and CrxE80A/A retinas showed positive RHO staining at P3 (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C and 6D with immunostaining.

claim: The detection of RHO protein in P3 CrxE80A mutant retinas indicates that photoreceptor differentiation program was precociously activated.
source: The detection of RHO protein in P3 CrxE80A mutant retinas indicates that photoreceptor differentiation program was precociously activated.
evidence: This is inferred from the early appearance of RHO protein.

claim: E80A and K88N mutations each perturbs CRX regulatory activity in a unique way.
source: Taken together, our results support a model that E80A and K88N mutations each perturbs CRX regulatory activity in a unique way, causes photoreceptor differentiation defects, and ultimately leads to distinct dominant disease phenotype that recapitulates human diseases.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive analysis of all data.

claim: E80A and K88N mutations cause photoreceptor differentiation defects.
source: Taken together, our results support a model that E80A and K88N mutations each perturbs CRX regulatory activity in a unique way, causes photoreceptor differentiation defects, and ultimately leads to distinct dominant disease phenotype that recapitulates human diseases.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive analysis of all data.

claim: E80A and K88N mutations ultimately lead to distinct dominant disease phenotype that recapitulates human diseases.
source: Taken together, our results support a model that E80A and K88N mutations each perturbs CRX regulatory activity in a unique way, causes photoreceptor differentiation defects, and ultimately leads to distinct dominant disease phenotype that recapitulates human diseases.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive analysis showing consistency with human phenotypes.

claim: CRX E80A is associated with increased transcriptional activity.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that missense mutations in the CRX HD, by either a loss- or gain-of-function mechanism, alter CRX target specificity and/or CRX transactivation activity.
evidence: This is shown by luciferase assays and gene expression data.

claim: CRX K88N has altered DNA-binding specificity.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that missense mutations in the CRX HD, by either a loss- or gain-of-function mechanism, alter CRX target specificity and/or CRX transactivation activity.
evidence: This is shown by Spec-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claim: Both CRX E80A and CRX K88N proteins impair photoreceptor gene expression.
source: These biochemical property changes impair CRX-mediated transcriptional regulation in vivo and lead to distinct morphological and functional deficits (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is shown by RNA-seq data.

claim: Both CRX E80A and CRX K88N proteins lead to distinct morphological and functional deficits.
source: These biochemical property changes impair CRX-mediated transcriptional regulation in vivo and lead to distinct morphological and functional deficits (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is shown by histology and ERG data.

claim: Both target specificity and regulatory activity precision at the canonical CRX targets are essential for proper photoreceptor development and functional maturation.
source: Thus, both target specificity and regulatory activity precision at the canonical CRX targets are essential for proper photoreceptor development and functional maturation.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive analysis of all mutants.

claim: Both CrxE80A and CrxK88N mouse models develop whorls and rosettes in the ONL by P21.
source: Despite the difference in molecular mechanisms, both CrxE80A and CrxK88N mouse models develop whorls and rosettes in the ONL by P21, which are not observed in degenerative CRX mouse models (Tran et al., 2014), suggesting distinct pathogenic mechanisms.
evidence: This is shown by histological analysis and comparison with previous models.

claim: Whorls and rosettes in the ONL are not observed in degenerative CRX mouse models.
source: Despite the difference in molecular mechanisms, both CrxE80A and CrxK88N mouse models develop whorls and rosettes in the ONL by P21, which are not observed in degenerative CRX mouse models (Tran et al., 2014), suggesting distinct pathogenic mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: The formation of whorls and rosettes suggests distinct pathogenic mechanisms from degenerative models.
source: Despite the difference in molecular mechanisms, both CrxE80A and CrxK88N mouse models develop whorls and rosettes in the ONL by P21, which are not observed in degenerative CRX mouse models (Tran et al., 2014), suggesting distinct pathogenic mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with previous models.

claim: CRX K88 residue is the major contributor to HD DNA-binding specificity.
source: Most distinctively, CRX K88 residue, at HD50 position, is the major contributor to HD DNA-binding specificity, with lysine making favorable interactions with both guanines in the CRX consensus TAATCC-binding site (Baird-Titus et al., 2006; Chaney et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Lysine at K88 position makes favorable interactions with both guanines in the CRX consensus TAATCC-binding site.
source: Most distinctively, CRX K88 residue, at HD50 position, is the major contributor to HD DNA-binding specificity, with lysine making favorable interactions with both guanines in the CRX consensus TAATCC-binding site (Baird-Titus et al., 2006; Chaney et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: CRX target specificity is critical for photoreceptor development fidelity.
source: Supporting the importance of K88 residue-mediated CRX target specificity in regulating photoreceptor development, CrxK88N retinas show more severe perturbations in photoreceptor gene expression and development than in loss-of-function mutant CrxR90W/W.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing the severity of phenotypes.

claim: CrxK88N/+ and CrxK88N/N mice display the most severe photoreceptor morphological deficits observed in any Crx mouse models.
source: CrxK88N/+ and CrxK88N/N mice display the most severe photoreceptor morphological deficits observed in any Crx mouse models and show absence of visual functions in young adults.
evidence: This is shown by histological and ERG analysis.

claim: CrxK88N/+ and CrxK88N/N mice show absence of visual functions in young adults.
source: CrxK88N/+ and CrxK88N/N mice display the most severe photoreceptor morphological deficits observed in any Crx mouse models and show absence of visual functions in young adults.
evidence: This is shown by ERG analysis.

claim: The severe CrxK88N phenotypes are attributed to both diminished activity at canonical CRX motifs and ectopic binding and transcriptional activity at N88 HD motifs.
source: It is likely that the severe CrxK88N phenotypes are attributed to both diminished activity at canonical CRX motifs and ectopic binding and transcriptional activity at N88 HD motifs.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq and gene expression data.

claim: CRX K88N activity at N88 HD motifs might ectopically activate genes whose expression prevents the progression of development or inactivate genes required for development.
source: Alternatively, these results suggest involvement of additional regulatory mechanisms: CRX K88N activity at N88 HD motifs might (1) ectopically activate genes whose expression prevents the progression of development or inactivate genes required for development
evidence: This is speculated based on the severity of the phenotype.

claim: CRX K88N activity at N88 HD motifs might interfere with other HD TFs that also recognize N88 HD motifs.
source: (2) interfere with other HD TFs that also recognize N88 HD motifs
evidence: This is speculated based on the altered DNA-binding specificity.

claim: CRX K88N activity at N88 HD motifs might lead to epigenetic alterations that antagonize normal CRX functions.
source: (3) lead to epigenetic alterations that antagonize normal CRX functions.
evidence: This is speculated as a possible mechanism.

claim: Many other HD containing TFs are expressed in developing mouse retina, including OTX2, RAX, VSX2, PAX6, SIX3/6, and LHX family.
source: Many other HD containing TFs are expressed in developing mouse retina, including OTX2, RAX, VSX2, PAX6, SIX3/6, and LHX family (Diacou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Alteration of CRX DNA-binding specificity could mis-regulate genes originally targeted by other HD TFs and lead to severe perturbations in the retinal gene regulatory networks.
source: Alteration of CRX DNA-binding specificity could mis-regulate genes originally targeted by these HD TFs and lead to severe perturbations in the retinal gene regulatory networks.
evidence: This is speculated based on the altered DNA-binding specificity.

claim: CRX R90 residue has been suggested to confer additional stability for the HD fold besides the core residues.
source: CRX R90 residue has been suggested to confer additional stability for the HD fold besides the core residues and make contacts with the DNA backbone through bases in the TAAT core motif (Baird-Titus et al., 2006; Chaney et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: CRX R90 residue makes contacts with the DNA backbone through bases in the TAAT core motif.
source: CRX R90 residue has been suggested to confer additional stability for the HD fold besides the core residues and make contacts with the DNA backbone through bases in the TAAT core motif (Baird-Titus et al., 2006; Chaney et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Substitution of the basic R90 residue with a bulky, neutral tryptophan (W) potentially reduces overall CRX HD stability.
source: Substitution of the basic R90 residue with a bulky, neutral tryptophan (W) potentially reduces overall CRX HD stability which in term reduces CRX HD DNA-binding affinity without affecting its binding preference.
evidence: This is inferred from structural considerations.

claim: R90W substitution reduces CRX HD DNA-binding affinity without affecting its binding preference.
source: Substitution of the basic R90 residue with a bulky, neutral tryptophan (W) potentially reduces overall CRX HD stability which in term reduces CRX HD DNA-binding affinity without affecting its binding preference.
evidence: This is inferred from Spec-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claim: The potential reduction in CRX HD–DNA complex stability is in line with the observation that R90W mutation abolishes CRX binding across the genome.
source: The potential reduction in CRX HD–DNA complex stability is in line with our observation that R90W mutation abolishes CRX binding across the genome resulting in global loss of CRX target gene activation.
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-seq data.

claim: CRX E80 residue plays a role in stabilizing the HD–DNA-binding complex through intramolecular interactions with other HD residues.
source: Structural studies suggest that CRX E80 residue plays a role in stabilizing the HD–DNA-binding complex through intramolecular interactions with other HD residues (Wilson et al., 1995; Chaney et al., 2005), yet functional validations await further experiments.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: E80A mutation could render HD–DNA interactions more promiscuous.
source: E80A mutation, replacing glutamic acid (E), which is acidic and polar, with alanine (A), which is neutral and non-polar, could render HD–DNA interactions more promiscuous as reflected in overall reduced magnitude of CRX E80A HD specificity (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is inferred from Spec-seq data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Regulatory sequences of many photoreceptor genes contain both consensus and non-consensus CRX motifs.
source: Regulatory sequences of many photoreceptor genes contain both consensus and non-consensus CRX motifs (Chen et al., 1997; Furukawa et al., 1997; Chen et al., 2002; Corbo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The more promiscuous CRX E80A–DNA interaction increases the likelihood of non-consensus CRX HD motifs being bound and activated resulting in overall increased transcriptional output.
source: It is likely that the more promiscuous CRX E80A–DNA interaction increases the likelihood of non-consensus CRX HD motifs being bound and activated resulting in overall increased transcriptional output (hyperactivity) as seen both in luciferase assays and in developing CrxE80A mouse retinas.
evidence: This is inferred from Spec-seq, luciferase, and RNA-seq data.

claim: The promiscuous TF-DNA-binding associated hyperactivity phenomenon has been observed in a dominant disease mouse model harboring a missense mutation in KLF1.
source: The promiscuous TF-DNA-binding associated hyperactivity phenomenon has also been observed in a dominant disease mouse model harboring a missense mutation in the zinc finger TF Krüppel-like factor-1 (KLF1) (Gillinder et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to another study.

claim: Photoreceptor differentiation is programmed via sequential and concerted gene expression programs within a defined time window.
source: Photoreceptor differentiation is programmed via sequential and concerted gene expression programs within a defined time window (Wang and Cepko, 2016; Brzezinski and Reh, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to developmental studies.

claim: CRX E80A hyperactivity precociously activates later stage genes in the absence of proper nuclear context and/or subcellular structures, which negatively impacts early events in photoreceptor differentiation.
source: One explanation for adult CrxE80A phenotypes is that CRX E80A hyperactivity precociously activates later stage genes in the absence of proper nuclear context and/or subcellular structures, which in turn negatively impacts early events in photoreceptor differentiation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the gene expression patterns and phenotypes.

claim: Cones undergo terminal differentiation to develop into cone subtypes – M- or S-cones – in a similar postnatal window as rods.
source: While cones undergo terminal differentiation to develop into cone subtypes – M- or S-cones – in a similar postnatal window as rods, they were born prenatally in mice within an earlier time window than rods.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cone development.

claim: Cones were born prenatally in mice within an earlier time window than rods.
source: While cones undergo terminal differentiation to develop into cone subtypes – M- or S-cones – in a similar postnatal window as rods, they were born prenatally in mice within an earlier time window than rods.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cone development.

claim: Cells expressing RXRγ were observed in CrxE80A retinas.
source: At an early postnatal age, cells expressing RXRγ, a ligand-dependent nuclear hormone receptor normally expressed in developing cones (Kaufman et al., 2019; Sapkota et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2001; Roberts et al., 2005), were observed in CrxE80A retinas, suggesting cone photoreceptors were born in these mutant retinas (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A with immunostaining.

claim: Cone photoreceptors were born in CrxE80A mutant retinas.
source: At an early postnatal age, cells expressing RXRγ, a ligand-dependent nuclear hormone receptor normally expressed in developing cones (Kaufman et al., 2019; Sapkota et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2001; Roberts et al., 2005), were observed in CrxE80A retinas, suggesting cone photoreceptors were born in these mutant retinas (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of RXRγ+ cells.

claim: CRX E80A hyperactivates the S-cone opsin promoter reporter pOpn1sw-luc.
source: Supporting this model, CRX E80A also hyperactivates the S-cone opsin promoter reporter pOpn1sw-luc (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B with luciferase assay data.

claim: Cones depend on a different repertoire of TFs than rods for subtype terminal differentiation.
source: It is known that cones depend on a different repertoire of TFs than rods for subtype terminal differentiation (Kaufman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a developmental study.

claim: Different point mutations at CRX E80 residue have been reported in dominant CoRD cases.
source: It is important to note that different point mutations at CRX E80 residue have been reported in dominant CoRD cases (ClinVar VCV000865803.1, VCV000007416.7, VCV000099599.6), emphasizing the importance of residue CRX E80 in regulating cone photoreceptor development.
evidence: This is supported by references to ClinVar database entries.

claim: Cones only make up a very small portion (3%) of photoreceptors in mouse retinas.
